title: He Knew He Would Raise Lazarus… So Why Did Jesus Weep?
paragraphs:
He Knew He Would Raise Lazarus… So Why Did Jesus Weep?
The Tears That Changed Everything: Understanding the Deep Meaning of Jesus Weeping at Lazarus’ Tomb and What It Reveals About the Heart of God
If there is one verse in all of Scripture that seems simple on the surface but becomes infinitely deeper the longer you stare at it, it is found in John 11:35.
Yet hidden inside those tears is one of the most breathtaking revelations of the heart of God ever recorded.
Because Jesus already knew what He was about to do.
He knew Lazarus would walk out of the tomb.
He knew death was about to lose.
He knew mourning would become celebration.
He knew the miracle before anyone else did.
That reality should stop every believer in their tracks.
Why would the Son of God cry over a problem He was about to solve?
Why would the Creator of life stand before a temporary grave and shed tears?
Why would the Resurrection Himself mourn?
To understand this moment, we must walk slowly into Bethany.
Because somewhere in this story, every one of us eventually finds ourselves.
A loss we never prepared for.
A season where heaven feels silent.
The story begins in John 11 when Lazarus becomes gravely ill. Lazarus was not merely an acquaintance of Jesus. Scripture specifically tells us:
“Now Jesus loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus.” (John 11:5)
Instead of rushing to Bethany, He stays where He is for two more days.
Hope seems buried beneath a stone.
How many believers have lived inside that feeling?
But the Gospel repeatedly teaches that God's delays are not God's denials.
What feels like abandonment is often preparation.
What looks like silence is often divine orchestration.
When Jesus finally arrives, Martha meets Him with words that countless believers have whispered through tears:
“Lord, if You had been here, my brother would not have died.” (John 11:21)
Mary eventually says the exact same thing.
Faith and heartbreak are colliding in the same sentence.
Yet Jesus answers with one of the most powerful declarations ever spoken:
“I am the resurrection and the life.” (John 11:25)
Notice what He does not say.
He does not say, “I can perform a resurrection.”
He does not say, “I know about resurrection.”

Ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ ἀνάστασις καὶ ἡ ζωή
(Egō eimi hē anastasis kai hē zōē)
“I AM the resurrection and the life.”
The phrase Ἐγώ εἰμι (Egō eimi) deliberately echoes God's self-revelation.
In Exodus 3:14, God reveals Himself to Moses in Hebrew:
Jesus is not merely offering comfort.
The One standing before the tomb is the God who spoke existence into being.
The One crying is the same One who hung every star.
The One grieving is the Author of life itself.
The deepest verse in human experience.
The Greek word used here is extraordinarily important.
John does not use the word describing loud public wailing.
He uses a word describing quiet tears.
The tears of someone whose heart has been pierced.
And this raises the question that has echoed through centuries.
Some suggest He cried because He loved Lazarus.
Every funeral hurts because every life matters.
But there is something even deeper happening here.
When Jesus arrives, He sees Mary weeping.
The consequences of sin's invasion into God's good creation.
John records that Jesus was “deeply moved.”
The phrase translated “deeply moved” comes from the Greek word:
In other words, Jesus is not merely sad.
He is confronting humanity's ancient enemy.
The tomb before Him represents everything sin brought into the world.
Every tear shed over a loved one.
Jesus stands before the devastation caused by sin and His soul is stirred with holy emotion.
His tears are not signs of weakness.
They are signs of divine compassion.
His tears reveal that God is not emotionally detached from human suffering.
Many people imagine God as distant.
God feels the weight of human sorrow.
The prophet Isaiah foretold this centuries earlier:
“He was despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.” (Isaiah 53:3)
Jesus did not merely observe grief.
This means something profoundly personal for every reader.
The tears Jesus shed at Lazarus' tomb reveal that God sees every tear you have ever cried.
“You have kept count of my tossings; put my tears in Your bottle.”
And Jesus proves that truth standing before Lazarus' tomb.
Yet there is another layer still.
Perhaps the most beautiful layer of all.
Jesus knew He would raise Lazarus.
Yet He still entered the grief before ending it.
Because love does not rush past pain.
Jesus did not say, “Stop crying. Everything will be fine.”
Before He changed their circumstances, He joined their suffering.
That is exactly what He still does today.
Many people want a God who immediately removes pain.
The Gospel offers something even greater.
A Savior who enters pain with us.
The cross itself would soon demonstrate this truth on an even grander scale.
At Calvary, Jesus would step into humanity's suffering completely.
The tears at Lazarus' tomb point forward to the blood at Calvary.
God loves sinners more than sinners understand.
And perhaps nowhere is that love more visible than in the theme that runs through all of Scripture.
Because Lazarus' story is ultimately our story.
Yet Jesus stands before our spiritual tombs just as He stood before Lazarus'.
Life enters where death once ruled.
That is your testimony if you belong to Christ.
The scandal of sin became the story of redemption.
The grave became the birthplace of resurrection.
The ending changed because Jesus arrived.
Maybe you are reading this carrying your own tomb.
Remember that the Savior who cried at Lazarus' tomb has not changed.
And He still calls dead things back to life.
The tears of Jesus were never the end of the story.
They were the beginning of a miracle.
And perhaps that is why this passage continues to grip hearts two thousand years later.
Because every believer lives somewhere between verse 35 and verse 44.
Between the tears and the resurrection.
Between the grief and the miracle.
Between the tomb and the breakthrough.
If this message stirred your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
What tomb are you trusting Jesus with right now?
Your testimony may become someone else's reason to keep believing.
Because sometimes the proof that God loves you is not that He stopped the tears... but that He cried beside you before He turned the page.
